sources.entry: JavaScript: _How to implement regular expressions in functional javascript using derivatives_

summary.title: Regular Expressions (Toy Regex Engine in JavaScript)
summary.one_liner: You learn how a regular expression engine can match strings using Brzozowski-style derivatives, implemented as a small purely functional JavaScript toy.
keywords: how to write a regexp matcher
takeaways: Regex matching can be done by repeatedly computing the derivative of a regex with respect to each input character, stopping on a match, a dead end, or the end of input.
Regex nodes can be represented as a linked list with alternation nodes, where a character node's derivative is its next node if the character matches, and NeverMatches otherwise.
Repetition is represented by a cyclic node that points back to its head, which requires side-effects to construct.
Naive full-match checking fails for regexes ending in a repetition, so the design adds matchEnd and canMatchMore methods to nodes to decide when a match is complete.
summary.summary: The article explains the theory behind one way to implement regular expressions: computing derivatives of a regex with respect to each input character. It then builds a toy engine in JavaScript in a mostly functional style, starting from the bottom layer of node classes (character, alternation, any-character, repetition) and working up to a friendlier API with Or, ZeroOrMore and Any, plus a compiler and an RE wrapper class. It walks through worked examples and a bug in the initial match function, which is fixed by adding matchEnd and canMatchMore methods. The toy supports grouping, alternation, repetition and literal/wildcard matching, with features like zero-width assertions, submatch extraction and substring search left as exercises.
